title: Extending separation logic to verify the xv6 OS kernel on RISC-V with AI agents
content:
Computer Science > Logic in Computer Science

Title:Extending concurrent separation logic to the hardware level to verify the xv6 OS kernel on RISC-V with AI agents
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:MachCSL is a framework for verifying system software, such as an OS kernel, on top of low-level semantics of a RISC-V computer, based on the Sail RISC-V semantics. The key idea behind MachCSL is to adapt concurrent separation logic, based on Iris, to reasoning about low-level hardware execution at the sub-instruction level: page-table translation, TLB, privilege levels, configuration registers, instruction fetch/decode/execute, traps and interrupts, DMA, shared memory, power failures, etc. Reasoning at this level of detail ensures that the system software correctly manages all of the hardware details.
Verifying software at this low level of abstraction is tedious, but LLM-based agents are capable of reasoning about such low-level details. As a case study, we verify the xv6 OS kernel (6,657 lines of C and assembly code), which provides a traditional Unix system call interface (processes, file system, file descriptors, and preemptive scheduling) and has substantial internal concurrency (multi-core support with fine-grained locking, shared memory, interrupts, DMA, etc.). In the verification process, we uncovered 11 bugs in the xv6 implementation, as well as one bug in the Sail RISC-V semantics, and one bug in Sail's Lean extraction. The verification effort took us 102 days, including the time to develop the MachCSL framework.
On top of the verified xv6 kernel, we prove a theorem about console-level behavior: e.g., if the user types echo hello world as input on the UART console, the only output the system can produce is hello world (if there are no crashes or other errors). This theorem covers both the kernel and the init, sh, echo, cat, grep, sync, and seccomp binaries in the initial file system image.

report.summary: MachCSL extends Iris-based concurrent separation logic down to RISC-V hardware semantics, using LLM agents to verify the xv6 kernel and find 13 bugs in 102 days.
report.background: Kernel verification has a long pedigree: seL4's refinement proof, CertiKOS, and frameworks built on concurrent separation logic such as Iris. Most of these proofs assume an idealized machine model, leaving page tables, TLBs, privilege levels, DMA, and interrupts outside the trusted base — or handled by large, hand-written refinement proofs. Meanwhile, RISC-V has acquired a rigorous formal ISA specification in Sail, and LLM-based agents have become surprisingly good at the tedious, detail-heavy work of interactive theorem proving. MachCSL sits at the intersection: it pushes separation-logic reasoning down to sub-instruction hardware execution, and leans on AI agents to make that level of detail economically feasible. xv6, MIT's teaching Unix kernel, is the natural case study — small enough to attempt, concurrent and hardware-facing enough to be interesting, and widely read by students and researchers.
key_points: MachCSL adapts Iris-style concurrent separation logic to reason at the sub-instruction level of a RISC-V machine, built on the Sail RISC-V semantics. That means page-table translation, TLB behavior, privilege levels, configuration registers, instruction fetch/decode/execute, traps, interrupts, DMA, shared memory, and even power failures all fall inside the proof, rather than being assumed away by an idealized machine model.

Reasoning at this granularity is notoriously tedious for humans, so the team used LLM-based agents to grind through low-level details. The full effort — writing the framework plus verifying the kernel — took 102 days, a striking figure given that comparable refinement proofs traditionally consume person-years and large teams.

Verification paid off in unexpected places: the team found 11 bugs in xv6 itself, plus one bug in the Sail RISC-V semantics and one bug in Sail's Lean extraction. Bugs in the specification and tooling show that end-to-end proofs audit the trusted base too, not just the software under test.

Beyond functional correctness, the paper proves a console-level theorem: if a user types 'echo hello world' on the UART console, the only possible output is 'hello world' absent crashes or errors. The theorem spans the kernel and the init, sh, echo, cat, grep, sync, and seccomp binaries in the initial file-system image — a genuine end-to-end systems property.

The verified target is full xv6 — 6,657 lines of C and assembly — with multi-core support, fine-grained locking, shared memory, interrupts, and DMA, preserving the traditional Unix system-call interface of processes, file descriptors, file systems, and preemptive scheduling.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a credible data point that LLM agents can contribute to machine-checked proofs of real systems code, not just benchmark lemmas — a path toward AI-assisted verification of hypervisors, drivers, and firmware. For kernel and systems developers, it argues that hardware-level details (TLBs, DMA, interrupts) can be brought inside the proof envelope, shrinking the trusted computing base; the Sail and Lean bugs are a reminder that formal specs need auditing too. For regular users, the payoff is indirect but real: operating systems whose safety and isolation claims hold all the way down to the silicon, with fewer silent memory-corruption and concurrency bugs. The 102-day figure also hints at a future where small teams can afford verification previously reserved for well-funded projects.
report.tools: Follow the Iris separation-logic framework (Coq/Rocq) for the proof foundation, the Sail language and the open RISC-V Sail model for ISA semantics, and Lean 4 for the extraction toolchain implicated in the reported bug. xv6-riscv on GitHub is the case-study kernel and easy to run under QEMU; seL4 and CertiKOS offer contrasting verification approaches. For agent-assisted proving, watch Lean/Coq copilot projects and emerging LLM-for-ITP tooling.
